name: Uma Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Uma. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. Could you start by walking me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm at Linden Hill by half five, which is a dairy and barley farm owned by a cooperative of about forty members. I feed the calves, scrape out the cubicles and help in the milking parlour, then in summer I drive the grain trailer at harvest. I was a school cook for twenty-eight years, so I'm still the new girl here at fifty-eight, and the young lads know more than me about most things. I love the calves, and I hate the early frost on the yard.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What made you switch to farm work so late?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The school kitchen went over to a catering firm that trucked in reheated trays, and I couldn't stand serving that to children. My grandparents had cows, and I always said I'd go back to animals before I got too old. Linden Hill pays well because the co-op signed a deal with the farmworkers' union, which I joined in my first week. Jonas, my partner, thinks I'm mad getting up at five when we've got the house paid off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. “Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right, so the clever computers stay mostly talk. That sounds like most of the gadgets I've seen come and go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I said about the reheated school dinners: a lot of noise and somebody selling something. At union meetings I'd tell people not to let the bosses use the word AI to squeeze our hours anyway. Nobody needs a chatbot to feed a calf.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means nothing much changes for me, and I'd be glad. My job is buckets, gates and a shovel, and the manager does the computer side. I've got about five more years in me, and in this picture I get them just as I planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my shifts, keep paying my union dues and keep putting a bit by each month, same as now. I'd keep stopping at sixty-three, when Jonas finishes his last bus route. Maybe I'd finally learn to back the trailer properly, because the lads still laugh at me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit smug, if I'm honest, because I never touched any of it. I'm not a worrier when the money's sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the bosses might use AI as an excuse. Is anything already squeezing your hours or pay at Linden Hill?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really, the co-op's been decent, and the union deal runs till 2029. The only grumble is milk prices, which go up and down whatever the computers do. Milk prices have kept me awake more nights than any robot, and I've only been in farming two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a younger worker asked you whether to learn these AI tools, what would you tell them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell young Pawel, who started the same month as me, to learn whatever keeps him in work, because he's got forty years ahead. I don't need to, at my age. I'd also tell him to join the union, which is the bit he keeps putting off.

say: AI is mostly **sales talk**, like every gadget I've seen come and go.
Bosses shouldn't use **AI as an excuse** to cut our hours anyway.
think: My job is **buckets and shovels**, so nothing much changes for me.
I get my **last five years** at Linden Hill exactly as planned.
do: Keep working her **usual shifts** and paying union dues.
Keep **saving monthly** and stop at **sixty-three** alongside Jonas.
feel: **Calm** and a little **smug** about never touching AI.
S0.quote: Milk prices have kept me awake more nights than any robot, and I've only been in farming two years.
fieldNote: Her **money worries** are about milk prices, not technology.
The **union deal** to 2029 gives her a sense of protection.
Her advice to a young colleague shows she sees AI as a **young person's problem**.

steps.text: Keep the calf-feeding and parlour shifts at Linden Hill until sixty-three
Keep paying farmworkers' union dues and attend the spring meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. “Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: So the office jobs get hit first and the robots come slowly. That's a different kettle of fish for my kids than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At the union I'd push for a written rule that nobody gets laid off for a machine without a year's notice and retraining. Online I don't post, but I'd sign every petition going. I'd say the co-op should share any savings with the workers, not just the members.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, the manager's paperwork changes and my shovel doesn't. The co-op might buy a feed robot that pushes up silage, and then they need one less pair of hands at five in the morning. I'm the most junior, so I'd be first in line, but I'd only lose a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the union rep, Marta, to get a no-redundancy clause into the 2029 deal now. I'd keep my head down and keep working, and I'd look at the dairy across the valley as a backup, since farms round here are always short of hands. I wouldn't touch any of the AI stuff myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy, more for others than for me. It's like watching a storm cross the next field.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said your kids. Who in your family would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tomas is an electrician, so he's fine, he'll be wiring the robots. My daughter Lena is a nurse, and the hospital already wants her typing notes into a tablet half the shift. My daughter became a nurse to look after people, not to babysit a computer that writes her notes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the feed robot did come, would you be willing to learn to run it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not, I'm not good with screens and I'd make a mess of it. I'd rather move to another farm that still needs someone to bottle-feed calves. There are plenty of those within twenty minutes of my house.

say: Nobody should be laid off for a machine without **a year's notice** and retraining.
The co-op should **share savings** with its workers, not just its members.
think: The manager's **paperwork** changes first, and my shovel stays the same.
I'm the **most junior**, so I'd go first if a feed robot came.
do: Ask union rep Marta for a **no-redundancy clause** in the 2029 deal.
Keep the **dairy across the valley** in mind as a backup job.
feel: **Uneasy**, more for her **children** than for herself.
S1.quote: My daughter became a nurse to look after people, not to babysit a computer that writes her notes.
fieldNote: She worries most about her **nurse daughter**, whose job has more screen work.
She would rather **change farms** than learn to run a robot.

steps.text: Ask the union rep to add a no-redundancy clause to the 2029 deal
Keep working her shifts and refuse to use the new software

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. “Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Goodness. And the robots three years after, so 2031, when I'd be sixty-three.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud at every union meeting: this is the time for the government to step in. A tax on the robots, a proper pension at sixty, and help for families. I'd be marching, which I've done twice in my life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it means the robots turn up the very year I planned to stop. The manager's ordering and milk records would go to the computer in 2028, and that's not my job. But by 2031 a robot that can scrape cubicles and feed calves would make me the first one out, probably a year or so early.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd sit down with Jonas and work out if we can both stop at sixty-two instead. I'd go to the regional union meetings and push for the robot tax. I'd keep every shift going until they tell me otherwise, and I'd move some of our savings out of the bank shares that the man at the branch talked us into.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, if I'm honest. Not for the money, we'd manage, but for the feeling of being pushed out of the one job I chose for myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the gap between the thinking AI in 2028 and the robots in 2031 mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means three years where the office goes strange and I'm still out with the calves. I'd spend my last three years at Linden Hill watching the robot salesmen walk round the yard with clipboards. That's three years to get the union ready, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd be fine for money but you're still anxious. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. We'd eat and pay the bills, Jonas has his bus pension. But I left a school I'd been at for twenty-eight years because something cold took it over, and I don't want that to happen twice.

say: The government has to step in with a **robot tax** and a pension at sixty.
I'd **march** and speak up at every union meeting.
think: The robots arrive in **2031**, the exact year I planned to stop.
As the junior, I'd be **pushed out early** once a robot can feed calves.
do: Plan with Jonas whether both can **stop at sixty-two**.
Push the **robot tax** at regional union meetings.
Move some savings out of **bank shares** they were sold.
feel: **Anxious** about being **pushed out** of a job she chose.
S2.quote: I'd spend my last three years at Linden Hill watching the robot salesmen walk round the yard with clipboards.
fieldNote: Money is secure through **Jonas's pension**, but the hurt is about losing chosen work.
Losing the **school kitchen** to a contractor shapes her fear of it happening again.
She sees the **three-year gap** as time to organise, not to retrain.

steps.text: Work out with Jonas whether both can stop work at sixty-two
Push a robot tax motion at the regional union meetings
Move part of the savings out of the bank shares
Join marches calling for a pension at sixty

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. “Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, and the robots in 2034. I'd be sixty-six by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as before: tax the robots and look after the people. But I'd say it a bit more calmly, because there's time to get the laws written properly. I'd want the union pushing on it from the first year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be gone from Linden Hill by 2034. I'd have my calves and my shovel right up to sixty-three. It's Lena and Tomas I'd be thinking about, and the young ones like Pawel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working to sixty-three as planned. I'd go to the union meetings and help write the letters to our member of parliament, because I'd have the time. And I'd tell Lena to keep some savings aside, since she has a mortgage and two little ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more like worrying about the weather for a harvest I won't be bringing in. I'd feel sorry for the lads who'll still be there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Pawel if this were the picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Pawel he has eight good years to learn the robots inside out, so he's the one fixing them instead of the one replaced. A robot on the farm in 2034 is young Pawel's (her workmate's) problem, not mine, because Pawel is only twenty-five. I'd still drag him to the union, mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your daughter at the kitchen table about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Lena to pay down that mortgage faster while she still has two incomes. Nurses won't vanish, but the hospital may cut the hours. I'd offer to help with the grandkids so she can do extra shifts.

The **union** should start pushing from the first year.
think: I'll have **retired** from Linden Hill before the robots turn up.
My worry is really for **my children** and young ones like Pawel.
do: Help the union write **letters to their MP**.
Help Lena with **childcare** so she can pay down her mortgage.
feel: **Uneasy**, like worrying about a **harvest** she won't bring in.
S3.quote: A robot on the farm in 2034 is young Pawel's (her workmate's) problem, not mine, because Pawel is only twenty-five.
fieldNote: The **five-year warning** moves her own risk past her retirement date.
Her concern for **young Pawel** shows her union instinct for others.
She turns worry into **family help**, offering childcare to her daughter.

steps.text: Keep working at Linden Hill until sixty-three as planned
Help the union write letters to their member of parliament
Look after the grandchildren so Lena can work extra shifts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. “Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.”

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, and robots in 2039. I'd be seventy-one and hopefully pottering in my garden.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to do it right, so there's no excuse if the government makes a mess of it. Retraining money, shorter hours, decent pensions. I'd say it at the union and to anyone in the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's nothing, I'm long retired by then. The only bit that touches me is whether the pension holds up and whether my kids are okay. Tomas will be fine, Lena maybe less so.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd do nothing different at work: calves, shovel, sixty-three, done. I'd keep up the union until I stop and then join the retired members' branch. I'd help Lena think about a nursing job that's still hands-on, like the care home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm for me, a little uneasy for the next lot. Mostly I'd feel glad to be the age I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the pension. Is that a real worry?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. If nobody's working, who pays in? But Jonas and I own the house and have savings, so we'd be all right even if it got trimmed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Looking back on all three fast pictures, what changes most for you between them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Just the date the robots turn up compared with my sixty-third birthday. If the robots come after my sixty-third birthday, I'll wave at them from the bus stop. If they come before, I'll be marching. The thinking computers never bother me on a dairy farm, because the robots are the ones that would take my shovel.

We need **retraining money**, shorter hours and decent pensions.

My only stake is the **pension** and how Lena and Tomas get on.

S4.quote: The thinking computers never bother me on a dairy farm, because the robots are the ones that would take my shovel.
fieldNote: The **robot date** against her retirement date decides her whole reaction.
A paid-off **house and savings** make pension worries small.

steps.text: Keep working at Linden Hill to sixty-three, then stop

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because the robots land right on my retirement year and I'd be pushed out of my chosen job early. What would help is a law that says a farm can't drop a worker for a robot without a year's notice and a fair payout, and a pension at sixty for people doing hard physical work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets the money the robots save. That's what I'd want to know. If the co-op saves wages, the workers should get a share, or it's just the school kitchen all over again.

headlineQuote: If the robots come after my sixty-third birthday, I'll wave at them from the bus stop. If they come before, I'll be marching.
portrait: A former **school cook** who started at a co-op dairy at fifty-six and is still the junior.
A committed **union member** who distrusts tech firms and never uses AI tools.
Calm in slow pictures because **retirement at sixty-three** comes before any robot.
Anxious in **AGI by 2028**, when robots arrive the year she planned to stop.
Answers threats through **the union and politics**, not by learning new tools.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with robots pushing her out of farm work just before **sixty-three**.
whatWouldHelp: A law requiring **a year's notice** and fair payouts before workers are replaced.
A **pension at sixty** for physical workers and a share of robot savings.
